title: Slicing and Extracting Parts of a String
summary: Teaches string.slice(start, end): zero-based positions, an exclusive end index, and how to compute the result length. The exercise truncates a tweet to 140 characters, with a condensed one-expression version.

concepts.heading: slice(start, end)
points: Syntax: string.slice(startIndex, endIndex). It must be called on a string or a variable holding one (name.slice(0, 3)); slice alone is meaningless.
Returns a new string; the original is unchanged. (Extra) That is true of all string methods because strings are immutable.
Indices count from 0, so in "Angela" A is position 0 and the last letter a is position 5 (the sixth character).
The start index is included, the end index is excluded: slice(0, 1) gives "A", slice(5, 6) gives "a", slice(0, 3) gives "Ang".
Quick length check: end minus start gives the number of characters returned (3 - 0 = 3; 5 - 1 = 4).
On "abc", slice(1, 3) returns "bc" because positions 1 and 2 are included and position 3 does not exist.
(Extra) If the end index is omitted, slice goes to the end of the string; negative numbers count back from the end; an end beyond the length is clamped, so a short text is not padded or errored.

concepts.heading: Editor shortcut
points: Cmd+/ (Mac) or Ctrl+/ (Windows) toggles comment on the selected lines, handy for switching old code off and on in the snippets editor.

concepts.heading: Enforcing a tweet limit
points: Instead of only reporting excess characters, cut the text down to the limit.
Prompt for text, then slice from 0 to 140 (140 - 0 = 140 characters).
A variable name can include digits but not start with one, hence tweetUnder140.
Variables here are only for readability: the whole thing collapses to a single alert(prompt("...").slice(0, 140)) expression because a function call can stand in for the value it returns.

code_examples.caption: slice examples
code_examples.code:
var name = "Angela";
name.slice(0, 1); // "A"
name.slice(5, 6); // "a"
name.slice(0, 3); // "Ang"
name.slice(1, 5); // "ngel" (5 - 1 = 4 characters)

Condensed version (same idea as reference repo 14.07, which limits to 10 characters)

task.name: Cut a tweet down to 140 characters
task.starting_point: Snippet containing the prompt for a tweet (from the earlier counter exercise).
task.goal: Alert back only the first 140 characters of whatever was entered.
steps: Prompt for text and keep it in a variable, tweet.
Test with a long pasted paragraph and check the result with .length.
Optional: merge into one line by replacing variables with the expressions they hold.
task.expected_result: An alert showing exactly the first 140 characters of the input.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 14 - Introduction to Javascript ES6/14.07 - Slicing and Extracting Parts of a String/script.js (author's variant: limit of 10 characters and a message with the count; fix punctuation typo in its alert)

pitfalls: Expecting the end index to be included.
Calling slice without a string in front of it.
Null from a dismissed prompt makes .slice throw an error.

playground.coverage: Covers slice(start, end), zero indexing, exclusive end, first 10 characters, first letter, negative indices, slice(5), and capitalising a name. Goes beyond the lecture.
gaps_and_ideas: Make the tweet-truncation exercise explicit (slice(0, 140) on a long pasted prompt answer), matching the lecture's main task.
Add the 'end minus start equals length' shortcut and a worked table for "Angela" with indices 0-5.
Add the Cmd/Ctrl+/ comment toggle tip.
Interactive demo: type a word and two index numbers and see highlighted characters selected, showing the exclusive end.
Add a task collapsing three lines into one nested expression.
